How ImageTo20KB Works

Everything below happens in your browser. Your image is not uploaded for compression.

1. Check the file

The file’s first bytes are inspected to confirm it is really a JPEG, PNG or WebP, and size and pixel limits are applied. Animated, SVG and HEIC files are rejected with an explanation.

2. Decode and resize

The image is decoded and drawn on a canvas at your chosen maximum dimensions, keeping the aspect ratio. Images are never enlarged.

3. Search for the best quality

For JPEG and WebP, the tool encodes at several quality levels using a bounded binary search and measures the actual size of each result. It keeps the highest quality that fits the target.

4. Shrink only if needed

If even the minimum quality is too large, dimensions are reduced step by step and the search repeats, up to fixed limits.

5. Report honestly

If the final file is at or below the target you see “target reached”. Otherwise you get the smallest result and a message saying it is above target. PNG is encoded once because it is lossless.

Why real measurement matters

A quality setting such as 70 does not mean a file will be a certain size. Two photos at the same setting can differ by a factor of ten in file size. That is why the tool always encodes, measures the actual bytes, and only then decides. One kilobyte is counted as 1,024 bytes, so 20KB means 20,480 bytes and 100KB means 102,400 bytes.

Quality first, then dimensions

Very low JPEG quality causes blocky patches and colour smearing. The tool therefore keeps quality at a reasonable level and prefers a somewhat smaller picture when the target is tight. It finds the largest dimensions that fit, then raises quality again to use any leftover space. If you must keep exact dimensions, tick "Keep dimensions" in Advanced settings and accept lower quality.

Better resizing

Reducing a big photo to a small one in one step can create jagged edges. The tool halves the picture in stages and does the final adjustment last, which tends to give a cleaner result.

How this compares with Squoosh image compression

People often search for "squoosh image compression" when they want a free in-browser compressor. Squoosh is an open-source project from Google Chrome Labs that lets you compare several codecs and adjust each setting by hand, which is powerful if you enjoy tuning. ImageTo20KB automates one common task, hitting a size in KB. If you already know the exact codec settings you want, use a manual tool. If a form just says "under 20KB", the presets here are quicker. We are not affiliated with Squoosh.

Format behaviour

JPEG and WebP are lossy, so quality can be searched. PNG is lossless, so the tool encodes it once and reports the size. If your browser cannot encode a format, it is not offered. The downloaded file always has the extension that matches its real format.

Batch processing and downloads

Several files can be processed with a small limit on how many run at once, which keeps phones responsive. Each file has its own status. If one fails, you can retry it or remove it, and the others carry on. A ZIP download includes only successful results and gives each file a unique safe name.

Memory and safety limits

Files over 50 MB or over 50 megapixels are rejected, because decoding them can exhaust a browser's memory. Temporary links created for previews are released when you remove a file or leave the page. Nothing in this process sends your image to a server.

What the tool does not do

It does not crop, rotate, remove backgrounds or edit metadata, and it cannot promise that a specific website will accept the output. Always check the destination's rules. Ready? Try compress image to 20KB or compress image to 100KB. Questions? See the FAQs.
